title: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)
hook: three days so dark "they saw not one another"; yet in Israel's homes there was light

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portion's first word, bo. Your line was come, not go: someone is already in the room. Today, the ninth plague.

During a power cut at night, the first thing most people do isn't look for a flashlight. It's call out. Are you okay? Where are you? Darkness doesn't only hide the furniture. It hides the people. The ninth plague is darkness, and the Torah describes it less like night and more like a weight. It came after the locusts, it lasted three days, and the most striking line about it isn't about the sky at all. It's about what people could no longer see in each other.
screen: `THE POWER CUT.` → `ARE YOU OKAY?` → `THE NINTH PLAGUE.`

segments.voice: Moses stretches out his hand toward heaven, and a thick darkness covers Egypt. The old Jewish translation calls it "darkness which may be felt." Darkness you could touch. Then comes the detail. For three days, "they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place." Not just the road. They couldn't see each other, and because of that, nobody got up. A teaching often told in Hasidic circles reads those two halves as cause and effect. The darkest darkness, it says, is when a person doesn't see his brother. Stop seeing the person next to you, and you can't move. You stay stuck in your place. The verse ends with a turn: "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings." The Torah doesn't explain how. Commentators offered many answers; the plain text stays quiet. But notice where the light was: in homes, among people. The midrash also wonders why the darkness lasted three days, and gives several reasons, none of them in the verse itself. What the verse gives is the picture: one land where nobody could see anybody, and homes where people could. A dark time can be a whole country's or one person's. Grief does it. Depression does it. A long illness, a lost job. The person inside often can't rise from their place. Someone else, with light, can see them.
screen: `DARKNESS WHICH MAY BE FELT.` · `THEY SAW NOT ONE ANOTHER.` · `NOT SEEING, SO NOT RISING.` · `LIGHT IN THEIR DWELLINGS.` · then, large: `SEE YOUR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Let a few faces come to mind and ask who's had the lights go out lately: a friend who's gone quiet, a neighbor after a loss, a relative who's stopped answering. Let one face stay, and without fixing anything, just see them properly, the way you'd call out in a power cut. If you pray, you can hold them there for a while.
Bo. Still our portion. Today its ninth plague: darkness so thick no one could see another person, and light in Israel's homes.
Your line: see your brother. Brother, sister, friend, stranger: whoever is sitting in the dark. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 334 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BO: THIS MONTH IS YOURS (EXODUS 12:1–2).`

howItsDone: The ten plagues are recited at the Passover seder, a drop of wine spilled for each, and darkness is the ninth. Jewish tradition counts visiting and checking on people who are ill or grieving, bikur cholim and comforting mourners, as a mitzvah.

notes: JPS 1917 Exodus 10:21 ('even darkness which may be felt') and 10:23 quoted from memory; KJV reads the same. Verify exact wording and punctuation.

The 'whoever doesn't see his brother can't rise from his place' teaching is widely attributed (often to the Chiddushei HaRim of Ger, sometimes others); the script says only 'often told in Hasidic circles'. A Keeper may supply the source.
Midrash on the length and reasons for the darkness (Shemot Rabbah 14; also Rashi on 10:22) mentioned only generally; confirm reference.
Hebrew in 10:21–22 is choshekh; 'afelah' also appears in 10:22. The original game uses choshekh.
Index carry 'see your brother' kept; the carry voice widens it to sister, friend, stranger.
